summary: Cattle Point Light on San Juan Island: a lens lantern on a post from 1888, a Navy radio compass station from 1921, and a concrete tower from 1935 beside American Camp.

lens.note: 1935: non-rotating 375 mm drum lens in the lantern; after automation, a 250 mm drum lens on a short mast (HistoryLink)

light.note: Light sits at 94 ft (HistoryLink); flashing white every four seconds (HistoryLink). Range: visible for seven miles (HistoryLink, unit not stated).

structures.note: Brass lens lantern on a post (HistoryLink)
34-foot octagonal concrete tower with a fog-signal building (HistoryLink; LighthouseFriends)

staffing.note: No full-time keeper from 1935; a contract light keeper tended the tower. Automated in the late 1950s (HistoryLink). The Navy radio compass station's sailors maintained the light from 1921 (LighthouseFriends; NPS).

access.note: Lighthouse closed to the public. It can be seen on foot by a short trail from the parking area near the end of Cattle Point Road (HistoryLink). USLHS: not open to the public.

visit.note: Cattle Point Interpretive Area and beach trail are open; the tower is closed (NPS; HistoryLink; LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard owns the lighthouse (LighthouseFriends; HistoryLink). Cattle Point is part of San Juan Islands National Monument (NPS).

events.note: Hudson's Bay Company's Belle Vue Farm set up; cattle and livestock unloaded at a dock at the point
Cattle Point first named on British Admiralty charts
Lighthouse Board picks four sites in the islands for major lights, Cattle Point among them
Lens lantern on a post; LighthouseFriends gives 1 October 1888 as the first showing
US Navy radio compass station built near the light; sailors take over maintenance of the light
34-foot octagonal concrete tower and fog-signal building replace the lantern; Navy compass station closed
New light: 1,500 candlepower, visible for seven miles (HistoryLink)
Exxon television commercial uses the tower, with a faux lantern room and roof added for filming; LighthouseFriends text dates it 1984, its photo caption 1978
Erosion threatens the foundation; Coast Guard emergency repairs in summer 2010; permanent repairs carried out afterwards

keepers.name: George Jakle
keepers.note: Maintained the lens lantern and was paid to do so (LighthouseFriends). HistoryLink: a soldier stationed at American Camp who stayed on the island and raised sheep. LighthouseFriends and the NPS: son of, or family descended from, an American Camp soldier. The sources disagree on whether he was himself a soldier. No years of service are given.

corrections.proposed: lens lantern on a post, built 1888 (replaced); octagonal concrete tower, built 1935, 10.4 m (34 ft), standing
corrections.why: The 1888 structure was a lens lantern on a post, not a tower (HistoryLink; LighthouseFriends). The 34-foot concrete tower dates from 1935.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Record 28.7 m agrees with HistoryLink's 94 ft (28.7 m) and is kept. Wikipedia's 29 m (95 ft) is within rounding and was not cited.

notes_for_editor: (1) Sources on the first light agree on 1888 and a lens lantern; LighthouseFriends alone gives the day (1 October). (2) Jakle: HistoryLink says he was a soldier at American Camp; LighthouseFriends says he was the son of one; the NPS says his family descended from one. Not resolved. No source gives his years of service, so none are given. (3) Lens: HistoryLink describes a 375 mm drum lens in 1935; the Wikipedia infobox says 'Fourth order Fresnel lens (removed)' (lead only, not cited). Not resolved. (4) No wrecks, storms or rescues tied to Cattle Point were found in the sources read; the corpus search of the Lighthouse Board reports 1891-1901, the Commissioner reports 1915-1922 and the Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1912-1939 found no 'Cattle Point' entry, and the newspaper searches turned up only local notices. (5) The Navy radio compass staff (1921-1935) and the 1935-on contract keeper are not named in any source read, so they are not in the roster. (6) Record: ownership 'unknown' should read U.S. Coast Guard (LighthouseFriends; HistoryLink), recorded in facts.agency rather than as a correction. (7) Record: 'Fl W 4s' and 28.7 m agree with HistoryLink. (8) The USLHS place record gives no keeper names. (9) Tool bug: roster.py crashes on this USLHS place (KeyError 'lon' in place_header), because the place has no longitude. The place was matched by name and printed nothing. The roster cannot be checked with the tool until the crash is fixed. (10) The HistoryLink essay is dated 2006 and the NPS page was last updated in 2022; the 2010 repairs and 1984 commercial come from LighthouseFriends, not from a primary record. (11) No photographs added. (12) Added on fact-check 2026-10-28: the 1912 item in the San Juan Islander is a new rural free delivery (R.F.D.) mail route from the Friday Harbor post office to Jakle's gate, not a supply route; the story now says so. The Exxon commercial is dated 1984 in LighthouseFriends' text but 1978 in a photo caption on the same page; the story states both. The 1935 light's 'seven miles' and 94 ft are the 1935 lamp's figures (HistoryLink), not a claim about the present light.
